title: What happens if a plane window breaks at 35,000 ft?

beats.text: If this window breaks at 35,000 feet, you'd have as little as 15 seconds. Here's why.
In movies, everyone gets sucked out and the plane goes down. Reality is different. But still scary.
Outside, the air is thin, and minus 67 degrees. Inside, it's pumped up so you can breathe.
That pushes on every window with over a thousand pounds. Like a piano leaning on it.
So each window has three layers. The outer one takes all the load.
The middle one is a backup. And this tiny hole keeps it that way.
beats.label: BLEED HOLE

beats.text: But what if two layers break?
In under a second, the air rushes out. The cabin fills with fog, and anything loose flies toward the hole.
You've been watching this for about half a minute. Up here, without oxygen, you could already be too confused to save yourself.
That's why the masks drop by themselves. And why you put yours on first.
Then the pilots dive to 10,000 feet, where you can breathe again. Planes are built for this, and pilots train for it.
And this really happened. In 1990, a cockpit window blew out at 17,000 feet.
The captain was pulled halfway out of the plane.
The crew held on to his legs for 20 minutes, until the co-pilot landed. Everyone survived. Even the captain.
So... window seat or aisle? Save this for your next flight, and follow Hoot for more.
